`qaqcmar` applies quality control flags to Water Quality data collected through the Centre for Marine Applied Research's (CMAR) [Coastal Monitoring Program](https://cmar.ca/coastal-monitoring-program/).

## Installation

You can install the development version of `qaqcmar` from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("centre-for-marine-applied-research/qaqcmar")
```

`qaqcmar` uses the CMAR-developed [`sensorstrings`](https://github.com/centre-for-marine-applied-research/sensorstrings) package (version 1.4.1 or later), which is installed automatically.

See [NEWS.md](NEWS.md) for the changes in each version. Version 2.0.0 changes some arguments and the format of the threshold and human in the loop tables.

## Background

### Coastal Monitoring Program

The Centre for Marine Applied Research ([CMAR](https://cmar.ca/)) coordinates an extensive [Coastal Monitoring Program](https://cmar.ca/coastal-monitoring-program/) to measure [Essential Ocean Variables](https://www.goosocean.org/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=14&Itemid=114) from around the coast of Nova Scotia, Canada. There are three main branches of the program: _Water Quality_, _Currents_, and _Waves_. Summary reports and full datasets for each branch can be viewed and downloaded from several sources, as outlined in the [CMAR Data Access Reference Sheet](https://cmar.ca/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2026/10/2026-10-13_data_access_ns.pdf).

### Quality Assurance and Quality Control

CMAR applies Quality Assurance (QA) and Quality Control (QC) processes to support the delivery of high quality data (Bushnell et al., 2019). QA processes are typically completed prior to sensor deployment (e.g., sensor calibration and validation), and are documented in a series of Standard Operating Procedures.

QC processes (e.g., automated data flags, manual review) are completed for each deployment after the data have been collected and compiled. CMAR has adapted the QARTOD (Quality Assurance / Quality Control of Real-Time Oceanographic Data) flagging scheme and associated tests. QARTOD provides a relatively simple yet informative rating scale, and is very well documented. QARTOD manuals provide codeable instructions for implementing recommended QC tests. QARTOD has been adopted by oceanographic organizations around the world, including the US Integrated Ocean Observing System (IOOS).

For more information on the QC tests and thresholds, visit the [CMAR Data Governance Website](https://centre-for-marine-applied-research.github.io/cmp-data-governance/pages/cmp_about.html).

### Flags

Each test gives every observation one of four flags:

| Flag | Label | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pass | The observation passed the test. |
| 2 | Not Evaluated | The test could not be applied (e.g., no thresholds for the variable, or not enough nearby observations). |
| 3 | Suspect/Of Interest | The observation is unusual. It may be poor quality, or it may be a real event. |
| 4 | Fail | The observation is very likely poor quality. |

### Tests

| Test | Function | What it checks |
|---|---|---|
| Gross range | `qc_test_grossrange()` | The observation is within the sensor's range and within a reasonable range for the variable. |
| Climatology | `qc_test_climatology()` | The observation is within the expected range for the variable and month. |
| Spike | `qc_test_spike()` | The observation is not much higher or lower than the observations on either side of it. |
| Rolling standard deviation | `qc_test_rolling_sd()` | The standard deviation of the observations in a rolling window (default 24 hours) is not unusually high. |
| Depth crosscheck | `qc_test_depth_crosscheck()` | The minimum measured depth of each sensor is close to its estimated depth (`sensor_depth_at_low_tide_m`). One flag for each deployment. |
| Human in the loop | `qc_test_human_in_loop()` | Flags assigned by a person after reviewing the automated flags. |

The default thresholds for each test are in the `thresholds` table. Most depend on the county where the data were collected, and some also depend on the sensor type or month.

## Example

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(qaqcmar)
library(sensorstrings)
```

### Example data

Consider simulated Water Quality data from January 1 to December 28, 2023, recorded by four sensors in Lunenburg County. (Note: these data were simulated to illustrate quality control processes and do not reflect expected profiles.)

```{r}
path <- system.file("testdata", package = "qaqcmar")

dat <- readRDS(file.path(path, "test_data_grossrange.RDS"))

kable(dat[1:5, ])
```

```{r fig1, fig.height=6}
ss_ggplot_variables(dat) + geom_point(size = 1)
```

### Apply one test

`qaqcmar` includes a separate function for each QC test. For example, `qc_test_grossrange()` applies the gross range test by adding a `grossrange_flag_<variable>` column for each variable in `dat`. The county is taken from the `county` column of `dat`, or can be given with the `county` argument.

```{r, message=FALSE}
dat_gr <- qc_test_grossrange(dat, county = "Lunenburg")

kable(dat_gr[1:5, ])
```

`qc_plot_flags()` returns a list of figures, coloured by flag, with one element for each variable and, within it, one for each test in `qc_tests`.

```{r fig2}
p <- qc_plot_flags(dat_gr, qc_tests = "grossrange", ncol = 2)

p$temperature_degree_c$grossrange
```

### Apply several tests

`qc_test_all()` applies the tests in `qc_tests` and returns one flag column for each test and variable. Here, all five automated tests are applied.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
dat2 <- readRDS(file.path(path, "test_data_rolling_sd.RDS"))

dat_qc <- dat2 |>
  qc_test_all(
    qc_tests = c(
      "climatology",
      "depth_crosscheck",
      "grossrange",
      "rolling_sd",
      "spike"
    )
  )

colnames(dat_qc)
```

`qc_assign_max_flag()` adds a `qc_flag_<variable>` column with the *worst* flag for each observation of each variable. The depth crosscheck flag is not included, because it is one value for the whole deployment.

```{r}
dat_qc <- qc_assign_max_flag(dat_qc)

kable(dat_qc[
  1:5,
  c(
    "timestamp_utc",
    "dissolved_oxygen_percent_saturation",
    "qc_flag_dissolved_oxygen_percent_saturation"
  )
])
```

`qc_summarise_flags()` counts the observations with each flag.

```{r}
dat_qc |>
  qc_summarise_flags() |>
  filter(qc_test == "qc", variable == "dissolved_oxygen_percent_saturation") |>
  kable()
```

```{r fig3}
p <- qc_plot_flags(dat_qc, qc_tests = "qc")

p$dissolved_oxygen_percent_saturation$qc
```

## Thresholds

To see the default thresholds for a test, filter the `thresholds` table. Rows with `county = NA` apply in every county.

```{r}
thresholds |>
  filter(
    qc_test == "grossrange",
    variable == "temperature_degree_c",
    is.na(county) | county == "Lunenburg"
  ) |>
  kable()
```

Each test also accepts a table of thresholds, e.g., `grossrange_table` for `qc_test_grossrange()`. A user table has a `variable` column and one column for each threshold, and optionally `sensor_type` and `month` columns. An `NA` in `sensor_type` or `month` (or no column) means the row applies to any sensor type or month. A sensor-specific row is used before an "any sensor" row.

```{r, message=FALSE}
my_grossrange <- data.frame(
  variable = "temperature_degree_c",
  sensor_type = c(NA, "vr2ar"),
  sensor_min = c(-5, -5),
  sensor_max = c(35, 40),
  user_min = c(-1, 0),
  user_max = c(25, 20)
)

dat_user <- qc_test_grossrange(dat, grossrange_table = my_grossrange)
```

## Human in the loop

After reviewing the automated flags, a person can assign flags with `qc_test_human_in_loop()`. Each row of `human_in_loop_table` flags the observations of one deployment:

* `variable` and `sensor_serial_number`: the variable and sensor to flag (`NA` flags every variable or every sensor).
* `timestamp_utc_min` and `timestamp_utc_max`: the first and last observation to flag (`NA` means the start or end of the deployment).
* `qc_test` and `qc_flag_value` (optional): only flag observations that this test gave this flag.
* `human_in_loop_flag_value` and `hil_comment`: the flag and comment to assign.

Rows for other deployments are ignored, so the whole table can be passed for every deployment.

```{r, message=FALSE}
hil_table <- data.frame(
  station = "lighthouse",
  deployment_range = "2023-Jan-01 to 2023-Jan-15",
  variable = "dissolved_oxygen_percent_saturation",
  sensor_serial_number = NA,
  timestamp_utc_min = as.POSIXct("2023-01-15 12:30", tz = "UTC"),
  timestamp_utc_max = NA,
  qc_test = "rolling_sd",
  qc_flag_value = 3,
  human_in_loop_flag_value = 4,
  hil_comment = "dissolved oxygen: biofouling"
)

dat_hil <- dat2 |>
  qc_test_rolling_sd() |>
  qc_test_human_in_loop(hil_table)

dat_hil |>
  count(human_in_loop_flag_dissolved_oxygen_percent_saturation, hil_comment) |>
  kable()
```
